Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: I found out my 6-year-old daughter isn’t biologically mine. What should I do? Should I continue raising her?
Answer: My girlfriend (who is a urologist) had a patient who found out he had a rare congenital disease in the weirdest of ways. His wife pushed him to go for a fourth kid, but she could not get pregnant. So she had him tested. And the semen sample revealed that he was born with a condition which disabled him to have babies from the very start. He had NO biological children on his own, as it turned out. But his wife still found a way to be impregnated on three separate occasions — a harlot hattrick, if you want — behind her husband’s back. So what did he do ? The answer is pretty simple — Since he deeply loved his three children, he continued raising, and loving them. But he ditched the wife 🙂 SOURCES: image taken from GIFer.

Question: Have you ever done anything that was actually innocent but came off to others as creepy or inappropriate?
Answer: We made a walk in the woods with school friends and my family for my birthday. I had just reached the fine age of 10, and I was to explain them a thing or two about mushrooms (a hobby of mine). [Pope Clement VII died from death cap poisoning in 1534. Just days before his death he affirmed that Michelangelo should paint The Last Judgment above the altar in the Sistine Chapel. The death cap had spoken once again.][1] At some point, I found a death cap — arguably the most poisonous mushroom in the world — and I explained them just how poisonous it was. And then I took a big bite out of it. My parents (who knew it really was a death cap) froze, and two of my friends starting crying, while the others were flabbergasted by why I just did. Then I spit it out again, and resumed the guided tour as if nothing happened — but for some reason the atmosphere had changed. Some of my friends creeped out and had been convinced that I would die. My explaining them (in all smiles) that “the trick is not to swallow” did not fare well with my parents either. And that basically ended my Mushroom Magic career. SOURCES: the footnoted site, and for the image: Workshop of Bronzino, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: What was the most memorable thing a patient has said while drifting into sleep under anesthesia?
Answer: My girlfriend was still an absoluter beginner, and this was one of her first serious cases as a trainee of a surgeon. Maybe the most serious case of all, come to think of it. People come to the Emergency Room all the time for minor reasons, and this patient was not much different. A bad stomach ache and vomiting — probably a bad case of stomach flu. On the other hand, he was also in his mid-seventies, so every minor variation on a standard condition had to be taken seriously (just like in every other patient). But he deteriorated at an unexpected pace, and somehow something else was going on. His vomiting got worse and worse, and it never seemed to stop. The abdominal pain was suddenly beyond control. The surgeon on call deciding on the spot to open this man up, because basically his instinct told him that they could not wait for medical imaging and the like. And that’s exactly what he told the patient’s wife, before the patient was wheeled into the OR. Before leaving his wife’s sight, the patient told her that he loved her (a standard thing), and that he felt really good now that he knew the surgeons would solve his problem, as minor as it was — “I’ll see you in an hour, darling. And then we can go back home again.” When the surgeon and his amateur trainee opened him up, they found out that his bowel was blue-ish black, and they immediately knew what was going on. So they looked at each other and closed him up again. A bad case of bowel infarction — and nothing could be done. He would die without waking up some time later. His wife didn’t have a clue. SOURCES: the image is my own.

Name: Thomas Cayne
Question: As a doctor, what is the bravest thing you've ever seen a patient do?
Answer: This was simply a woman who wanted a baby, and nothing could stop her. So she wanted her husband’s sperm to be checked once again because something was going on. Something was dead wrong. And there was. Because his sperm sample was dead. They did not find a single living sperm cell, and what was even more surprising: it had always been that way. It must have, since it turned out that he was subsequently diagnosed with a rare congenital disorder that made him infertile from the start — he had always been infertile. So why was this woman’s insistence the bravest thing you've ever seen a patient do ? Because they already had three children. That is to say, she had three children, and her husband believed they were his biological children. But now it turned out that none of them were his own. Yet back in Egypt — where they had lived prior moving to Europe — she had found mysterious ways in getting pregnant, despite her husband’s congenital twist, whom she did not know of. So back in Egypt, she had found a source of viable sperm. And even now — even when the doctor had made it clear that her husband never was a biological father and never would be — she kept insisting. Because besides being incredibly brave, she was also another thing — Incredibly stupid. SOURCES: GIF taken from GIFER.

Question: What would happen if a patient refused intimate treatment/ care from nursing staff? How would that be documented and how would that patient be viewed?
Answer: This was a middle-aged patient who had entered the Emergency Room with a broken hip, in a lot of pain. He needed to rest and stay still before he would have an operation, and the orthopedist warned the nurses that this guy might be a bit stubborn, and had to be taken care of cautiously. Within the first hour of waiting, the patient became outraged that he was in a hospital, and he demanded to leave the hospital, because “there was NOTHING wrong with him !” The nurses reminded him that he had broken his hip, and that he must stay in bed until surgery — which he vehemently denied. He then screamed that he was leaving the hospital ASAP, and jumped off the hospital bed (and screamed like he had never screamed before). What would happen if a patient refused intimate treatment / care from nursing staff ? How would that be documented and how would that patient be viewed ? The patient’s hip was splintered, and he would need many surgeries in the future to walk (fairly) well again. His case was especially shocking and unpredictable, since next-to-no patient would jump off the bed with a broken hip ? On the other hand — this patient had young-onset dementia, of course. SOURCES: X-ray of the pelvis of an 86 year old male patient with a fractured hip. Image by Du Cane Medical Imaging. (Through Google Images.)
